extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of natural history/evolutionary biology; general educated public interested in sexual selection
extracted.subtask_description: A book-chapter discussion of sexual selection, sexual differences, and the origin of traits (physical, mental, vocal, and ornamental) in humans and other animals. Uses ethnographic, anatomical, and comparative-animal evidence to articulate principles by which sexual selection and related inheritance operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of battle (male–male competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Male contests for females (fighting/wrestling/competition) have been a primary cause of selection for strength and other male characters; winners leave more offspring and thus transmit such traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by ethnographic cases (Australians, some North American Indians, Guanas) where men wrestle or fight for women; analogized to male fights in higher Quadrumana and the presence/reversion of projecting canine teeth as vestiges of former weaponry. Includes examples where men delay marriage until able to win rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of jaws and teeth through disuse and correlation/economy of growth
rubrics_metrics.description: As human ancestors used hands and arms more for fighting and other tasks, jaws and teeth were used less and consequently reduced in size by disuse and correlated growth economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains disappearance or reduction of canine teeth in males compared with other primates; parallels cited with male ruminants whose canines are reduced when horns develop. Reversion (occasionally projecting canines) is presented as evidence of former state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation/augmentation of greater male strength by sexual and natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater male size, broader shoulders, more developed muscles, and greater pugnacity in humans are chiefly inherited from half-human male ancestors and preserved/augmented by success in struggle for life and contests for wives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues these differences are not primarily due to harder adult labor by men (women in barbarous societies work as hard) but due to selection during savagery and continued selection pressures during manhood; civilised change in selection regimes noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection as a cause of differences in mental powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in mental disposition (e.g., greater male energy, perseverance, courage; greater female tenderness and intuition) have been shaped in large part by sexual selection acting chiefly during maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with other animals (bull/cow, stallion/mare, male/female apes). Mental faculties valuable in contests (observation, reason, invention, imagination) were tested and selected during manhood and thus transmitted more to male offspring. Cites Galton's law of deviation, J.S. Mill, and observations on puberty and eunuchs as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of transmission by age and sex (timing of trait acquisition affects inheritance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters acquired late in life tend to be transmitted chiefly to the same sex at the corresponding age; characters acquired early in life tend to be transmitted to both sexes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a general rule with exceptions. Used to argue why traits developed during adult male contests would be passed more to males. Implication: adult training might cause sex-limited inheritance; equal early education for boys and girls would not necessarily erase adult sex differences under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal organ differences inherited and influenced by sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in voice (male vocal cords longer; larynx differences) are likely inherited from progenitors and influenced by long-continued use of the voice by males under excitement of love, rage, and jealousy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anatomical evidence cited (vocal cord length, effects of emasculation). Racial differences and examples from Quadrumana (gibbons) where males produce loud/musical voices. Notes lack of exhaustive natural observations for many species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical faculties evolved primarily in relation to courtship
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity for producing and appreciating musical notes and rhythm likely originated as a sexual/adaptive trait used during courtship to charm the opposite sex, and thus was subject to sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative evidence: insects' stridulation (often male), bird song, amphibian/fish vocalizations in breeding season, gibbon singing, singing rodents, archaeological flutes. Discusses alternative views (e.g., Spencer's claim that musical cadence derives from emotional speech) and argues music preceded emotive speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological basis for perception of musical notes in animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory systems (ear structures) can analyze sounds into component vibrations, enabling discrimination of musical notes; this capacity is present across a range of animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological and observational support: Helmholtz on acoustics, auditory hairs in crustaceans and insects, spiders attracted to music, dogs howling at particular notes, seals responding to music, etc. Used to rebut objections about evolving sensitivity to musical tones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music evokes emotions linked to courtship and social functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Music and rhythm arouse tenderness, love, devotion, triumph, and milder passions (not horror/fear), and these emotional associations originate in ancient courtship uses of music and are reinforced by inherited associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from human cultures (Chinese annals, negro song in Africa), comparative notes on birds/monkeys using tone to express emotions; posits music as linked to deep-seated inherited emotional responses from mating contexts, which explains music’s power in oratory and ritual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of beauty and ornamentation in mate choice (cultural manifestations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human mate choice has long been influenced by external appearance; in primeval/savage contexts, attention to personal ornamentation and bodily modification is pervasive and likely affected sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethnographic details: extensive ornamentation, painting, tattooing, teeth filing/staining, head shaping, ear/lip/nostril piercings, deliberate bodily deformation across cultures. Cites Mantegazza, Waitz, Humboldt, and others as sources documenting worldwide practices.
